questions.q: How is STRING_SPLIT used in a query, compared to a scalar function?
options: Only as an argument to another aggregate function
As a scalar function returning one comma-separated string
Only inside a WHERE clause
As a table-valued function, used with FROM, not in the SELECT list
questions.explain: STRING_SPLIT returns a rowset — one row per piece — so it's used in FROM like any other table-valued function.

questions.q: What is the single column name STRING_SPLIT always returns (without enable_ordinal)?
options: value
item
result
piece
questions.explain: STRING_SPLIT's output column is always named value, regardless of the input string's content.

questions.q: Why might real usage wrap STRING_SPLIT's output in TRIM(value)?
options: STRING_SPLIT adds a trailing separator to every value
STRING_SPLIT returns values in all uppercase
The split happens exactly on the separator character, so values after the first can retain a leading space from the original string
TRIM is required for STRING_SPLIT to function at all
questions.explain: STRING_SPLIT doesn't trim whitespace automatically, so a string like 'Red, Green, Blue' split on ',' leaves leading spaces on later pieces.

questions.q: What does the enable_ordinal parameter add when set to 1?
options: An ordinal column giving each piece's 1-based position in the original string
Automatic alphabetical sorting of the output
A column counting the total number of pieces
A column converting each piece to uppercase
questions.explain: enable_ordinal (SQL Server 2022+) adds a reliable position column you can ORDER BY to reproduce the original order.

questions.q: Without enable_ordinal, what is guaranteed about STRING_SPLIT's row order?
options: Nothing — the order is not guaranteed
Rows always come back in the exact order they appeared in the original string
Rows always come back in reverse order
Rows always come back sorted alphabetically
questions.explain: Without the ordinal column, STRING_SPLIT makes no promise about the order rows are returned in.
